The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model

Ivan Jacob Agaloos Pesigan

2026-11-01

Source: vignettes/ou.Rmd
ou.Rmd

Overview

The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model is a continuous-time model for variables that are pulled back toward an equilibrium level after they are pushed away from it, for example, mood returning to a person’s usual level after a stressful event. Continuous time means the model describes change at every moment, not only at the occasions we measure, so the same parameters apply whether measurements are one hour or one day apart, and the spacing can differ between occasions.

The model is a state space model with two parts: a measurement model that links the observed variables to the latent (unobserved) states, and a dynamic model, here a stochastic differential equation, that describes how the latent states change over time.

This tutorial does three things:

  1. It writes the multivariate OU model as a state space model.
  2. It simulates data from the model with SimSSMOUFixed(), with every individual sharing the same parameters.
  3. It fits the model to the simulated data with the dynr package and compares the estimates with the values used to simulate the data.

No prior knowledge of state space models is needed. The vignettes on the vector autoregressive model and the state space model cover the discrete-time versions.

Model

The measurement model is given by \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{y}_{i, t} = \boldsymbol{\nu} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{i, t}, \quad \mathrm{with} \quad \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{i, t} \sim \mathcal{N} \left( \mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Theta} \right) \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{y}_{i, t}\), \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t}\), and \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{i, t}\) are random variables and \(\boldsymbol{\nu}\), \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\), and \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) are model parameters. \(\mathbf{y}_{i, t}\) represents a vector of observed random variables, \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t}\) a vector of latent random variables, and \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{i, t}\) a vector of random measurement errors, at time \(t\) and individual \(i\). \(\boldsymbol{\nu}\) denotes a vector of intercepts, \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) a matrix of factor loadings, and \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) the covariance matrix of \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\).

In words, each observed variable is an intercept plus a weighted combination of the latent variables plus measurement error. The latent variables \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t}\) are the quantities we care about (for example, a person’s true stress level), and the observed variables \(\mathbf{y}_{i, t}\) are noisy measurements of them. Separating measurement error from true change is the main reason to use a state space model: measurement error affects only the occasion it occurs on, while changes in the latent variables carry over in time.

An alternative representation of the measurement error is given by \[\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{i, t} = \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{\frac{1}{2}} \mathbf{z}_{i, t}, \quad \mathrm{with} \quad \mathbf{z}_{i, t} \sim \mathcal{N} \left( \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I} \right) \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{z}_{i, t}\) is a vector of independent standard normal random variables and \(\left( \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{\frac{1}{2}} \right) \left( \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{\frac{1}{2}} \right)^{\prime} = \boldsymbol{\Theta}\) .

The dynamic structure is given by \[\begin{equation} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t} = \boldsymbol{\Phi} \left( \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t} - \boldsymbol{\mu} \right) \mathrm{d}t + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\frac{1}{2}} \mathrm{d} \mathbf{W}_{i, t} \end{equation}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) is the long-term mean or equilibrium level, \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) is the rate of mean reversion, determining how quickly the variable returns to its mean, \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is the matrix of volatility or randomness in the process, and \(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{W}\) is a Wiener process or Brownian motion, which represents random fluctuations.

In words, \(\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t}\) is the change in the latent variables over a very short time \(\mathrm{d}t\). The change has two parts: a pull toward the equilibrium \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\), proportional to the distance \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t} - \boldsymbol{\mu}\), and random fluctuations with covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) per unit time.

  • With this sign convention, a diagonal element \(\phi_{jj}\) is negative for a variable that returns to its equilibrium. The more negative it is, the faster the return.
  • An off-diagonal element \(\phi_{jk}\) is the effect of the distance of variable \(k\) from its equilibrium on the rate of change of variable \(j\). As in the discrete-time models, the row is the outcome and the column is the predictor.

For the process to settle around \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\), all eigenvalues of \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) must have negative real parts.

Over a time interval \(\Delta t\), the OU model implies a discrete-time vector autoregressive model with transition matrix \(\boldsymbol{\beta} = \exp \left( \boldsymbol{\Phi} \Delta t \right)\), the matrix exponential. SimSSMOUFixed() uses this exact discretization to simulate the data, so no approximation error is introduced.

Data Generation

Notation

Let \(t = 200\) be the number of time points and \(n = 10\) be the number of individuals.

Let the measurement model intercept vector \(\boldsymbol{\nu}\) be given by

\[\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{\nu} = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ \end{array} \right) . \end{equation}\]

Let the factor loadings matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) be given by

\[\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \left( \begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{array} \right) . \end{equation}\]

Let the measurement error covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) be given by

\[\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{\Theta} = \left( \begin{array}{ccc} 0.2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.2 \\ \end{array} \right) . \end{equation}\]

With \(\boldsymbol{\nu} = \mathbf{0}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{I}\), each observed variable measures one latent variable, and \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) adds measurement error with variance 0.2 to each.

Let the initial condition \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{0}\) be given by

\[\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{\eta}_{0} \sim \mathcal{N} \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\eta} \mid 0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\eta} \mid 0} \right) \end{equation}\]

\[\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\eta} \mid 0} = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ \end{array} \right) \end{equation}\]

\[\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\eta} \mid 0} = \left( \begin{array}{ccc} 0.3425148 & 0.3296023 & 0.0343817 \\ 0.3296023 & 0.5664625 & 0.2545955 \\ 0.0343817 & 0.2545955 & 0.2999909 \\ \end{array} \right) . \end{equation}\]

Let the long-term mean vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) be given by

\[\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{\mu} = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ \end{array} \right) . \end{equation}\]

Let the rate of mean reversion matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) be given by

\[\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{\Phi} = \left( \begin{array}{ccc} -0.357 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.771 & -0.511 & 0 \\ -0.45 & 0.729 & -0.693 \\ \end{array} \right) . \end{equation}\]

Read the columns as predictors and the rows as outcomes. The diagonal elements are all negative, so each variable returns to its equilibrium. In addition, \(\eta_{1}\) pushes up the change in \(\eta_{2}\) (0.771), \(\eta_{2}\) pushes up the change in \(\eta_{3}\) (0.729), and \(\eta_{1}\) pushes down the change in \(\eta_{3}\) (-0.45). Because \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) is lower triangular, its eigenvalues are its diagonal elements, all negative, so the process is stable.

Let the dynamic process noise covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) be given by

\[\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \left( \begin{array}{ccc} 0.2445556 & 0.0220159 & -0.0500476 \\ 0.0220159 & 0.070678 & 0.0153946 \\ -0.0500476 & 0.0153946 & 0.0755306 \\ \end{array} \right) . \end{equation}\]

Let \(\Delta t = 0.1\).

The data are measured every 0.1 time units. For example, if the time unit is one day, the 200 occasions span 19.9 days.

The initial condition describes where each individual starts. Here, the mean vector and covariance matrix of \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{0}\) are the model-implied mean and covariance of the stable process, computed with LinSDEMeanEta() and LinSDECovEta(), so the data are stationary from the first time point.

Visualizing the Dynamics Without Measurement Error and Process Noise (n = 5 with Different Initial Condition)

To see what \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) alone does, we first simulate five individuals with the process noise and the measurement error set to zero. Each individual starts at a different point, and the trajectories return to the equilibrium at a speed set by \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\).

Using the SimSSMOUFixed Function from the simStateSpace Package to Simulate Data

Now we add the process noise and the measurement error and simulate the full data set. as.data.frame() returns the data in long format, one row per individual and time point, with the columns id, time, y1, y2, and y3. The time column holds the actual measurement times (0, 0.1, 0.2, and so on), which the continuous-time model uses.

library(simStateSpace)
sim <- SimSSMOUFixed(
  n = n,
  time = time,
  delta_t = delta_t,
  mu0 = mu0,
  sigma0_l = sigma0_l,
  mu = mu,
  phi = phi,
  sigma_l = sigma_l,
  nu = nu,
  lambda = lambda,
  theta_l = theta_l,
  type = 0
)
data <- as.data.frame(sim)
head(data)

Model Fitting

We fit the model with dynr, which estimates state space models by maximum likelihood. For continuous-time models, dynr uses the time between measurements to get the implied discrete-time model for each interval, then applies the Kalman filter.

A dynr model is built from pieces that match the equations above: the data, the initial condition, the measurement model, the dynamic model, and the noise. Each parameter gets a name (for example, phi_2_1 for \(\phi_{21}\)`), and the same name used in two places means one shared parameter. The starting values are set to the population values for convenience; with real data, they would be rough guesses.

Prepare Data

Tell dynr which columns hold the individual, the time, and the observed variables.

dynr_data <- dynr::dynr.data(
  dataframe = data,
  id = "id",
  time = "time",
  observed = c("y1", "y2", "y3")
)

Prepare Initial Condition

The mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\eta} \mid 0}\) and covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{\eta} \mid 0}\) of the initial state are estimated. The covariance matrix is symmetric, so sigma0_2_1 appears both above and below the diagonal.

dynr_initial <- dynr::prep.initial(
  values.inistate = mu0,
  params.inistate = c("mu0_1_1", "mu0_2_1", "mu0_3_1"),
  values.inicov = sigma0,
  params.inicov = matrix(
    data = c(
      "sigma0_1_1", "sigma0_2_1", "sigma0_3_1",
      "sigma0_2_1", "sigma0_2_2", "sigma0_3_2",
      "sigma0_3_1", "sigma0_3_2", "sigma0_3_3"
    ),
    nrow = 3
  )
)

Prepare Measurement Model

The loadings \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) are an identity matrix with no free parameters ("fixed").

dynr_measurement <- dynr::prep.measurement(
  values.load = diag(3),
  params.load = matrix(data = "fixed", nrow = 3, ncol = 3),
  state.names = c("eta_1", "eta_2", "eta_3"),
  obs.names = c("y1", "y2", "y3")
)

Prepare Dynamic Process

Each formula is the rate of change of one latent variable: the effects \(\phi_{jk}\) of the distances of the three latent variables from their equilibria \(\mu_{k}\). isContinuousTime = TRUE makes this a continuous-time model.

dynr_dynamics <- dynr::prep.formulaDynamics(
  formula = list(  
    eta_1 ~ (phi_1_1 * (eta_1 - mu_1_1)) + (phi_1_2 * (eta_2 - mu_2_1)) + (phi_1_3 * (eta_3 - mu_3_1)),
    eta_2 ~ (phi_2_1 * (eta_1 - mu_1_1)) + (phi_2_2 * (eta_2 - mu_2_1)) + (phi_2_3 * (eta_3 - mu_3_1)),
    eta_3 ~ (phi_3_1 * (eta_1 - mu_1_1)) + (phi_3_2 * (eta_2 - mu_2_1)) + (phi_3_3 * (eta_3 - mu_3_1))
  ),
  startval = c(
    mu_1_1 = mu[1], mu_2_1 = mu[2], mu_3_1 = mu[3],
    phi_1_1 = phi[1, 1], phi_1_2 = phi[1, 2], phi_1_3 = phi[1, 3],
    phi_2_1 = phi[2, 1], phi_2_2 = phi[2, 2], phi_2_3 = phi[2, 3],
    phi_3_1 = phi[3, 1], phi_3_2 = phi[3, 2], phi_3_3 = phi[3, 3]
  ),
  isContinuousTime = TRUE
)

Prepare Process Noise

The diffusion covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is estimated in full. The measurement error covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) is diagonal: the three error variances are estimated, and the error covariances are fixed at zero.

dynr_noise <- dynr::prep.noise(
  values.latent = sigma,
  params.latent = matrix(
    data = c(
      "sigma_1_1", "sigma_2_1", "sigma_3_1",
      "sigma_2_1", "sigma_2_2", "sigma_3_2",
      "sigma_3_1", "sigma_3_2", "sigma_3_3"
    ),
    nrow = 3
  ),
  values.observed = theta,
  params.observed = matrix(
    data = c(
      "theta_1_1", "fixed", "fixed",
      "fixed", "theta_2_2", "fixed",
      "fixed", "fixed", "theta_3_3"
    ),
    nrow = 3
  )
)

Prepare the Model

The pieces are put together into one model. dynr writes the model as C code to outfile and compiles it.

model <- dynr::dynr.model(
  data = dynr_data,
  initial = dynr_initial,
  measurement = dynr_measurement,
  dynamics = dynr_dynamics,
  noise = dynr_noise,
  outfile = "ou.c"
)

Add lower and upper bounds on the elements of \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) to keep the optimizer away from implausible values.

model$lb[
  c(
    "phi_1_1",
    "phi_1_2",
    "phi_1_3",
    "phi_2_1",
    "phi_2_2",
    "phi_2_3",
    "phi_3_1",
    "phi_3_2",
    "phi_3_3"
  )
] <- -1.5
model$ub[
  c(
    "phi_1_1",
    "phi_1_2",
    "phi_1_3",
    "phi_2_1",
    "phi_2_2",
    "phi_2_3",
    "phi_3_1",
    "phi_3_2",
    "phi_3_3"
  )
] <- +1.5

The plot below shows the model equations with the parameter names.

Fit the Model 

results <- dynr::dynr.cook(
  model,
  debug_flag = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

Parameter Estimates

The estimates arranged as the matrices in the model, to compare with the population values in the Data Generation section. The last matrix, beta_var1_hat, is \(\exp \left( \hat{\boldsymbol{\Phi}} \right)\), the implied discrete-time transition matrix over one time unit.

Table of Parameters and Estimates

The table below puts each population value used to simulate the data next to its estimate. Bias is the estimate minus the population value. Because the model is fitted to a single simulated data set, this is the error of one estimate, not a Monte Carlo bias, which would average over many replications. The 95% confidence interval is the Wald interval, \(\hat{\theta} \pm 1.96 \times \mathrm{SE}\), and Covers shows whether it contains the population value.

EstimatesTable <- function(population, estimate, se) {
  z <- stats::qnorm(p = 0.975)
  ll <- estimate - z * se
  ul <- estimate + z * se
  data.frame(
    Parameter = names(population),
    Population = unname(population),
    Estimate = unname(estimate),
    SE = unname(se),
    Bias = unname(estimate - population),
    `2.5%` = unname(ll),
    `97.5%` = unname(ul),
    Covers = unname(population >= ll & population <= ul),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}
estimates <- coef(results)
se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(results)))
# the population value for each dynr parameter name,
# for example, "beta_1_2" is beta[1, 2] and "mu0_2_1" is mu0[2]
population <- vapply(
  X = strsplit(x = names(estimates), split = "_"),
  FUN = function(x) {
    as.matrix(get(x[1]))[as.integer(x[2]), as.integer(x[3])]
  },
  FUN.VALUE = numeric(1)
)
names(population) <- names(estimates)
knitr::kable(
  x = EstimatesTable(
    population = population,
    estimate = estimates,
    se = se
  ),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Population values and dynr estimates (one simulated data set)"
)
